Appendix A Research Workflow and Linked Records

DiscoveryRSI develops hypotheses comprising a scientific claim, investigation plan, decision criteria, and alternative explanations. This appendix describes the roles and records connecting hypothesis development to task delivery and subsequent learning.

A.1 Research Objects and Agent Roles

A hypothesis version is one recorded proposal; a revision links it to its predecessor. Crossover can introduce several parents, so the research tree is generally a directed acyclic graph. A development path follows ordered hypothesis versions; a research run contains the complete graph and its decisions. An agent trajectory records one agent invocation, including instructions, actions, and observations. Development paths and agent trajectories are distinct evaluation and training units.

Lead chooses directions, parents, operations, and selections. Generation proposes hypotheses; Evolution develops or repairs them. Critique provides blinded preferences, Progress assesses revisions against ancestry, and Compiler translates selected plans into Harbor tasks. Evolve and repair retain an existing direction, crossover combines directions, and restart opens a new question. Shared context can inform a restart without creating parentage.

A.2 Record Types and Provenance

The record layer links hypotheses to evidence, data, contributions, and execution. Ancestry records scientific development; evidence reuse and execution dependencies are separate relations. Table 2 summarizes the retained records.

Registry entries and filesystem artifacts implement these relationships. Source records retain retrieval time and available publication metadata separately. A provenance link establishes recorded use or production; scientific assessment determines how the material supports or limits a claim.

A.3 From Contributions to Executable Investigations

Credit preparation links an assessed hypothesis to producing, supporting, and coordinating agent trajectories. Publication identity, original drafts, artifact hashes, and event order distinguish original work from later quotation or reuse. These links supply the contributor pools in Equation 18. Unresolved associations receive no allocated share.

For example, Generation may propose a comparison, Evolution may revise it after inspecting evidence, and Lead may supply the assignment that enabled that work. Their records can identify supported actions across several trajectories. Contribution allocation determines each trajectory’s weight; target selection determines which of its assistant outputs receive supervision (Appendices B and C).

A selected computational investigation is compiled into a Harbor task containing its inputs, environment, required outputs, and verification checks. Compilation preserves the population or biological system, comparisons, discriminating outcomes, and decision criteria. Unavailable measurements and wet-lab experiments remain explicit dependencies. Compilation and readiness checks assess the computational package; completed execution and scientific assessment establish what evidence the investigation supplies.

A.4 Harness Replay and Rediscovery

DiscoveryRSI uses Codex and Claude Code for sessions, context management, filesystem access, and tool execution (OpenAI, 2026; Anthropic, 2026). Research adapters connect these facilities to agent roles, shared records, computation, and task delivery. Harness changes concern coordination, evidence access, review timing, and research allocation.

Diagnosis and replay.

Diagnostic runs hold the checkpoint and harness fixed. Linked decisions and execution records distinguish scientific-plan failures from tool failures, lost artifacts, and premature closure. Candidate repairs address evidence reuse, handoffs, retries, or completion checks; these examples do not constitute ablation results.

Replay preserves observations, tool access, and memory at the restored point. Alternatives require recorded continuations or new execution from a compatible state; ancestry alone supplies no counterfactual outcomes. This use of experience relates to Dream-RSI’s exploration-policy perspective (Zheng et al., 2026).

Acceptance and renewed investigation.

Harness comparisons hold the checkpoint, inputs, data access, and resource limits fixed. Model and harness candidates are assessed separately and jointly before deployment on fresh investigations (Algorithm 1).

Appendix B Hypothesis Credit Optimization

Hypothesis credit optimization converts scientific assessments into weighted supervision for documented research contributions. The procedure first estimates relative hypothesis preference, then assigns hypothesis weights, allocates contributor shares, limits credit within scientific families, and balances the training objective. Bayesian preference inference and contribution allocation are distinct steps.

B.1 Pairwise Preference Assessment

The preference model summarizes blinded pairwise Critique outcomes under a common scientific rubric. Its posterior describes relative preference strength; contributor attribution is determined separately from provenance.

The runtime collects blinded pairwise Critique outcomes: preference for A or B, a tie, or insufficient evidence. To derive the preference posterior, treat each versioned hypothesis as the rated entity in TrueSkill (Herbrich et al., 2006). Its latent quantity zhz_{h} represents preference strength under the scientific critique rubric, rather than an actor’s personal skill. For one compatible comparison population, take Gaussian priors and noisy comparison performances:

zh∼𝒩⁡(μh,0,σh,02),th,e=zh+ϵh,e,ϵh,e∼𝒩⁡(0,β2).z_{h}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{h,0},\sigma_{h,0}^{2}),\qquad t_{h,e}=z_{h}+\epsilon_{h,e},\qquad\epsilon_{h,e}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\beta^{2}). (8)

For comparison e=(a,b,oe)e=(a,b,o_{e}), the observed outcome depends on De=ta,e−tb,eD_{e}=t_{a,e}-t_{b,e}: A is preferred when De>εD_{e}>\varepsilon, B when De<−εD_{e}<-\varepsilon, and a tie when |De|≤ε|D_{e}|\leq\varepsilon. Here β\beta models performance noise and ε\varepsilon is the draw margin. With Δ​z=za−zb\Delta z=z_{a}-z_{b} and standard normal CDF Φ\Phi, integrating out performance noise gives

P⁡(A∣za,zb)\displaystyle P(A\mid z_{a},z_{b}) =Φ⁡(Δ​z−ε2​β),\displaystyle=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta z-\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2}\beta}\right), (9)
P⁡(B∣za,zb)\displaystyle P(B\mid z_{a},z_{b}) =Φ⁡(−Δ​z−ε2​β),\displaystyle=\Phi\!\left(\frac{-\Delta z-\varepsilon}{\sqrt{2}\beta}\right),
P⁡(tie∣za,zb)\displaystyle P(\mathrm{tie}\mid z_{a},z_{b}) =Φ⁡(ε−Δ​z2​β)−Φ⁡(−ε−Δ​z2​β).\displaystyle=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon-\Delta z}{\sqrt{2}\beta}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{-\varepsilon-\Delta z}{\sqrt{2}\beta}\right).

Insufficient evidence is an abstention and supplies no preference-likelihood factor. Under the comparison model’s conditional-independence assumption, Bayes’ rule yields the joint posterior

p⁡(𝐳∣𝒟cmp)=1Z​∏h𝒩⁡(zh,μh,0,σh,02)​∏e∈𝒟cmpP⁡(oe∣zae,zbe),p(\mathbf{z}\mid\mathcal{D}_{\rm cmp})=\frac{1}{Z}\prod_{h}\mathcal{N}(z_{h};\mu_{h,0},\sigma_{h,0}^{2})\prod_{e\in\mathcal{D}_{\rm cmp}}P(o_{e}\mid z_{a_{e}},z_{b_{e}}), (10)

where ZZ is the evidence normalizer. Pairwise factors couple hypotheses, so this joint posterior is generally neither Gaussian nor factorized. TrueSkill uses approximate message passing and Gaussian moment matching to retain tractable marginal beliefs. Stored online updates summarize the evidence available at their update time; they are reused without claiming an exact batch re-inference of the complete comparison graph.

How a comparison changes the posterior.

For a single decisive A-preferred comparison with independent Gaussian incoming beliefs, let

m=μa−μb,c2=σa2+σb2+2​β2,u=m−εc,V⁡(u)=ϕ⁡(u)Φ⁡(u),W⁡(u)=V⁡(u)​[V⁡(u)+u],m=\mu_{a}-\mu_{b},\quad c^{2}=\sigma_{a}^{2}+\sigma_{b}^{2}+2\beta^{2},\quad u=\frac{m-\varepsilon}{c},\quad V(u)=\frac{\phi(u)}{\Phi(u)},\quad W(u)=V(u)\bigl[V(u)+u\bigr], (11)

with standard normal density ϕ\phi. Before observing the outcome, D∼𝒩⁡(m,c2)D\sim\mathcal{N}(m,c^{2}). Conditioning on D>εD>\varepsilon truncates this Gaussian, giving 𝔼⁡[D∣A]=m+c​V​(u)\mathbb{E}[D\mid A]=m+cV(u) and Var⁡(D∣A)=c2​[1−W⁡(u)]\operatorname{Var}(D\mid A)=c^{2}[1-W(u)]. Gaussian conditioning transfers these moments to the latent hypotheses:

μa′\displaystyle\mu_{a}^{\prime} =μa+σa2c​V​(u),\displaystyle=\mu_{a}+\frac{\sigma_{a}^{2}}{c}V(u), μb′\displaystyle\mu_{b}^{\prime} =μb−σb2c​V​(u),\displaystyle=\mu_{b}-\frac{\sigma_{b}^{2}}{c}V(u), (12)
(σa′)2\displaystyle(\sigma_{a}^{\prime})^{2} =σa2​[1−σa2c2​W​(u)],\displaystyle=\sigma_{a}^{2}\!\left[1-\frac{\sigma_{a}^{2}}{c^{2}}W(u)\right], (σb′)2\displaystyle(\sigma_{b}^{\prime})^{2} =σb2​[1−σb2c2​W​(u)].\displaystyle=\sigma_{b}^{2}\!\left[1-\frac{\sigma_{b}^{2}}{c^{2}}W(u)\right]. (13)

These are the exact marginal first two moments for this single Gaussian-input comparison; retaining Gaussian beliefs is the approximation. A tie instead uses a two-sided truncated Gaussian. In a larger or sequential comparison graph, message schedules and Gaussian projection determine the stored approximation. Versioned runtime priors, noise, draw margin, and any dynamics variance remain part of the rating provenance; the static derivation does not silently replace those settings.

The stored marginals summarize relative preference strength within compatible source-snapshot, dataset, rubric, and connected comparison strata. Reviewer bias, scientific uncertainty, and dependence between repeated critiques are not fully represented by the Gaussian variance. Separate ancestor-aware Progress judgments supply transition evidence.

B.2 Hypothesis Weights

For a rated hypothesis, define a conservative ranking statistic and its tie-aware within-stratum rank:

sh\displaystyle s_{h} =μh−κ​σh,\displaystyle=\mu_{h}-\kappa\sigma_{h}, (14)
rh\displaystyle r_{h} =∑k∈𝒮𝟏[sk<sh]+12∑k∈𝒮𝟏[sk=sh]|𝒮|.\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{1}[s_{k}<s_{h}]+\tfrac{1}{2}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{1}[s_{k}=s_{h}]}{|\mathcal{S}|}. (15)

Under the Gaussian marginal approximation, shs_{h} is the Φ⁡(−κ)\Phi(-\kappa) posterior quantile; for κ=2\kappa=2, approximately 2.3%2.3\% of the modeled preference mass lies below it. This is a conservative statistic of rubric-conditioned preference. A singleton has rank 1/21/2, supplying no relative ordering. Let nhn_{h} be the effective comparison count. Two reliability factors damp the contribution of sparse or uncertain ratings:

ρhcov=nhnh+ν,ρhunc=11+σh/σref.\rho_{h}^{\rm cov}=\frac{n_{h}}{n_{h}+\nu},\qquad\rho_{h}^{\rm unc}=\frac{1}{1+\sigma_{h}/\sigma_{\rm ref}}. (16)

Let vhv_{h} indicate a recorded valid assessment and at least one effective comparison, with no recorded marginal-repetition judgment. Let php_{h} indicate a recorded substantive-progress or necessary-repair judgment. The bounded outcome transformation is given in Equation 17. Validity here means a coherent, assessable research design under the stored rubric, not experimental confirmation. The gate controls eligibility for this weak-supervision route. A missing rating or assessment remains an unknown outcome; zero assigned loss is not a negative scientific label. A valid hypothesis motivated by a supported null result remains eligible.

qh=vh​min⁡{qmax,qmin+(qmax−qmin)​rh​ρhcov​ρhunc+λp​ph}.q_{h}=v_{h}\min\!\left\{q_{\max},\;q_{\min}+(q_{\max}-q_{\min})r_{h}\rho_{h}^{\rm cov}\rho_{h}^{\rm unc}+\lambda_{p}p_{h}\right\}. (17)

Equation (17) is our bounded transformation of a preference posterior, not a quantity inferred by TrueSkill. The ranking statistic and uncertainty factor both penalize uncertainty; comparison count also correlates with posterior concentration. Their individual effects require ablation. A Progress bonus supplements the outcome weight without changing the TrueSkill posterior.

B.3 Contributor Shares and Provenance

We construct an auditable contribution graph whose edges identify an agent invocation’s relationship to a hypothesis. Direct publication requires matching publisher, episode, and creation-time provenance. Documented production or support can additionally be recovered from original prepublication proposal text, an exact draft-revision promotion record, or emitted supporting-file bytes whose hash and original path match the frozen candidate record. Lead coordination requires a contributing committed work assignment or publication/promotion record. Merely sharing an episode, appearing in an ancestry graph, or completing a worker invocation creates no credit edge. These links establish recorded association and production provenance; they do not establish sole authorship or the artifact’s scientific correctness.

For hypothesis hh, let LhL_{h} contain verified coordination trajectories and PhP_{h} contain direct production or documented supporting trajectories. Each trajectory belongs to at most one pool for a given hypothesis. With coordination fraction γ\gamma, define

αi​h={γ/|Lh|,i∈Lh,(1−γ)/|Ph|,i∈Ph,0,otherwise.∑iαi​h≤1.\alpha_{ih}=\begin{cases}\gamma/|L_{h}|,&i\in L_{h},\\ (1-\gamma)/|P_{h}|,&i\in P_{h},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\qquad\sum_{i}\alpha_{ih}\leq 1. (18)

Only nonempty pools are evaluated. If a contributor pool is missing, its share remains unallocated rather than being transferred to a convenient recipient. A Lead-only publication with unresolved authorship therefore receives the coordination share alone. Conversely, documented Lead production can enter PhP_{h}: the rule follows contribution function rather than a fixed role label.

For example, one coordinating Lead, one Generation publisher, and one Evolution trajectory with documented supporting work receive fractions 0.20.2, 0.40.4, and 0.40.4 under the implemented γ=0.2\gamma=0.2 policy. This allocation reaches work that need not register its own hypothesis. However, the fractions are a fixed responsibility prior, not a Bayesian posterior over actors or a counterfactual estimate of their marginal contribution. The TrueSkill marginal informs qhq_{h} through our explicit transformation; provenance supplies αi​h\alpha_{ih}. Critique votes cannot independently certify the correctness of those same critique outputs, and successful compilation cannot certify scientific fidelity. Such roles require their own evidence before receiving direct imitation targets.

B.4 Scientific-Family Credit Limits

Duplicate registrations do not receive additional scientific credit. We suppress exact duplicate proposal-credit events within a source snapshot and dataset. Local ancestry families Floc​(h)F_{\rm loc}(h) also receive a bounded outcome budget:

q~h=qh​min⁡{1,Cloc∑k∈Floc​(h)qk},ui​h=αi​h​q~h.\widetilde{q}_{h}=q_{h}\min\!\left\{1,\frac{C_{\rm loc}}{\sum_{k\in F_{\rm loc}(h)}q_{k}}\right\},\qquad u_{ih}=\alpha_{ih}\widetilde{q}_{h}. (19)

The local sum covers rated comparison nodes, including imported anchors when present; only generated hypotheses with contributor evidence allocate training credit. Global scientific families FglobF_{\rm glob} join recorded ancestry and compatible candidate or exact-proposal identities across snapshots. Their allocated credit is capped before forming a trajectory weight:

dF=min⁡{1,Cglob∑h∈F∑iui​h}.d_{F}=\min\!\left\{1,\frac{C_{\rm glob}}{\sum_{h\in F}\sum_{i}u_{ih}}\right\}. (20)

The final allocation from hypothesis hh to trajectory ii is bi​h=dFglob​(h)​ui​hb_{ih}=d_{F_{\rm glob}(h)}u_{ih}, and the trajectory weight is wi=min⁡(Wmax,∑hbi​h)w_{i}=\min(W_{\max},\sum_{h}b_{ih}). For a local family with zero total weight, the local cap factor is defined as one. For a zero-mass family, the cap factor is defined as one and allocated credit remains zero. These budgets limit the credit assigned to repeated versions of the same scientific question. They are pre-normalization credit constraints; subsequent domain and group balancing determines their relative influence in the final objective. Unresolved semantic duplication remains an audit limitation rather than an assumed solved problem.

B.5 Objective Balancing

Let gig_{i} identify a conservative shared-memory group, closed over campaign memory, ancestry, resumed trajectories, and recovered duplicates; these balancing groups are distinct from the scientific credit families above. For domain dd, let 𝒢d\mathcal{G}_{d} contain groups with retained targets and let ηd\eta_{d} be its desired objective mass. The fixed trajectory coefficient and intended update are

ωi=ηdi|𝒢di|wi∑k:dk=di,gk=giwk,∑dηd=1.\omega_{i}=\frac{\eta_{d_{i}}}{|\mathcal{G}_{d_{i}}|}\frac{w_{i}}{\sum_{k:\,d_{k}=d_{i},\,g_{k}=g_{i}}w_{k}},\qquad\sum_{d}\eta_{d}=1. (21)

All sums in Equation 21 concern retained trajectories with positive target mass. Coefficients and denominators are fixed from the frozen training release and are not renormalized within individual minibatches. This prevents transcript length alone from determining a trajectory’s loss weight. The coefficients allocate objective mass, not guaranteed shares of gradient norm. Initialization and optimization settings are reported in Appendix C.

B.6 Allocation Parameters

These constants specify the implemented allocation recipe; they are not estimates of causal contribution or empirically optimal hyperparameters. The uniform local credit cancels in the per-trajectory mean. Domain balancing is separate from scientific-quality ranking; a percentile within one stratum is not a universal cross-domain utility scale.

B.7 Credit Conservation

Proposition 1 (Pre-normalization credit conservation)

Fix deduplicated hypothesis-credit events and scientific-family assignments. Assume nonnegative hypothesis weights, positive budgets, and contributor shares satisfying ∑iαi​h≤1\sum_{i}\alpha_{ih}\leq 1. Under the local and global scaling rules,

∑ibi​h≤q~h,∑h∈F∑ibi​h≤Cglob,0≤wi≤Wmax\sum_{i}b_{ih}\leq\widetilde{q}_{h},\qquad\sum_{h\in F}\sum_{i}b_{ih}\leq C_{\rm glob},\qquad 0\leq w_{i}\leq W_{\max}

for each global scientific family FF. Missing contributor shares remain unallocated.

Proof.

Fix deduplicated credit events and a partition into global scientific families, with nonnegative weights, positive budgets, and 0≤γ≤10\leq\gamma\leq 1. Every cap factor belongs to [0,1][0,1]. The mutually exclusive contributor pools give ∑iαi​h≤1\sum_{i}\alpha_{ih}\leq 1, hence

∑ibi​h=dFglob​(h)​q~h​∑iαi​h≤q~h.\sum_{i}b_{ih}=d_{F_{\rm glob}(h)}\widetilde{q}_{h}\sum_{i}\alpha_{ih}\leq\widetilde{q}_{h}. (22)

For a global family FF, let UF=∑h∈F,iui​hU_{F}=\sum_{h\in F,i}u_{ih}. If UF>0U_{F}>0, then

∑h∈F,ibi​h=min⁡(1,Cglob/UF)​UF=min⁡(UF,Cglob)≤Cglob.\sum_{h\in F,i}b_{ih}=\min(1,C_{\rm glob}/U_{F})U_{F}=\min(U_{F},C_{\rm glob})\leq C_{\rm glob}. (23)

If UF=0U_{F}=0, all its allocations vanish. Similarly, the local scaling gives ∑h∈Flocq~h≤Cloc\sum_{h\in F_{\rm loc}}\widetilde{q}_{h}\leq C_{\rm loc} for each fixed local family. Nonnegativity and the trajectory cap yield 0≤wi≤Wmax0\leq w_{i}\leq W_{\max}. Missing contributor pools do not enter αi​h\alpha_{ih} and their reserved shares remain unallocated. This proves Proposition 1. The result holds before objective balancing; group normalization can change relative family influence and supplies no corresponding bound on gradient magnitude.

Appendix C Training Data and Implementation

This appendix documents the data and optimization used for full-parameter fine-tuning of DiscoveryRSI-27B. An agent trajectory is one recorded agent invocation, rather than a path through the hypothesis tree. Only supported assistant outputs receive direct loss; other retained tokens provide context.

C.1 Trajectory Collection and Selection

The source collection contains 15,792 research trajectories. Structural review identifies 13,270 reviewable agent trajectories, of which 13,269 pass export-integrity verification. Attribution identifies 2,432 agent trajectories with eligible supervision targets. Native-template tokenization retains 2,397 agent trajectories; 35 agent trajectories with unsupported mid-conversation developer messages remain excluded from the training export.

Lead, Generation, and Evolution account for 26.4%, 35.9%, and 37.6% of retained training trajectories, respectively. Critique, Compiler, and Progress records remain available as sources or context but receive no direct supervision. Exclusion from supervision indicates insufficient support under the attribution policy and does not imply that a role or trajectory lacks scientific value.

C.2 Supervision and Optimization

Scientific assessments and documented contributions determine fixed trajectory weights. Supervision targets supported assistant responses and tool-call arguments. Tool observations, failed actions, repeated context, and unsupported actions receive zero direct loss. For trajectory ii, let ωi\omega_{i} denote its fixed weight, ci​tc_{it} the supervision credit assigned to token tt, and Mi=∑tci​tM_{i}=\sum_{t}c_{it} its supervised mass. The implemented objective is

ℒcredit(θ)=−∑iωiMi∑tci​tlogπθ(ai​t∣xi​t).\mathcal{L}_{\rm credit}(\theta)=-\sum_{i}\frac{\omega_{i}}{M_{i}}\sum_{t}c_{it}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{it}\mid x_{it}). (24)

Weights and normalization factors are frozen before optimization. Domain balancing assigns 90% of the objective weight to life-science trajectories and 10% to battery-research trajectories. The objective uses offline weighted supervision; it does not involve online policy optimization.

The maximum training window is 262,144 tokens. Seven trajectories require multiple windows, producing 2,404 windows from 2,397 unique trajectories. Windows preserve canonical turn and tool-batch boundaries. Repeated initial and left context receives zero loss, and all windows from a trajectory share its supervision denominator and optimizer batch. The retained trajectories contain 304,424,899 tokens before window preparation. The final training sequences contain 291,121,000 tokens and preserve all 6,177,605 supervised targets. These totals refer to different preparation stages; the main text reports the final training-sequence count.

C.3 Training Configuration

Training uses full-parameter language-model fine-tuning with BF16 precision, Adam, a learning rate of 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}, and a global batch size of 16. One epoch completes in 150 optimizer steps. The distributed configuration uses 64 GPUs with tensor parallelism 4, context parallelism 8, and data parallelism 2. The final batch is padded with zero-loss entries to preserve the nominal batch normalization.

C.4 Serialization and Target Selection

Each trajectory retains its source identifier, original messages and tool definitions, linked hypotheses, contribution evidence, and exposure metadata. A token mask records eligible original assistant outputs and zero-loss positions. Instructions and tool observations remain context; known failed actions, repeated context, and unavailable reasoning placeholders receive zero direct loss. Serialization preserves instruction order and excludes future information from earlier contexts. Unsupported instruction sequences are omitted from the training export while their source records remain available.

The data preparation groups shared memory, ancestry, resumed interactions, and recovered duplicates before assigning balancing coefficients. These groups are distinct from the scientific families used to cap hypothesis credit. Targets are counted once across windows, and each trajectory retains one denominator. The fixed token coefficient under uniform trajectory sampling is N​ωi/MiN\omega_{i}/M_{i}, where N=2,397N=2{,}397 and MiM_{i} is the trajectory’s total supervised mass. Zero-loss padding preserves the nominal batch size at the end of the epoch.

The implemented token credit is constant at ci​t=0.5c_{it}=0.5 on eligible targets and zero elsewhere. This positive constant cancels between the numerator and MiM_{i}, giving the eligible-token mean in Eq. (4). Thus the main-text objective and Eq. (24) describe the same normalization. The weights specify relative loss contributions, not guaranteed shares of gradient magnitude.

Preparation checks cover source integrity, token/mask alignment, unique target coverage, fixed trajectory denominators, and domain-weight accounting. They validate the training representation; scientific correctness is assessed separately. In particular, conserving supervised targets and credit does not establish that the underlying hypothesis is scientifically supported. The source records and private research artifacts are not distributed with this supplement.

C.5 Windowing: Preserved Targets and Conditional Equivalence

Proposition 2 (Objective preservation under windowing)

Let UiU_{i} be the eligible target positions of trajectory ii, with |Ui|>0|U_{i}|>0, and let {Ui​w}w\{U_{iw}\}_{w} partition UiU_{i}. If each target retains its original conditioning context, all windows use the same fixed coefficient ωi\omega_{i}, and normalization uses |Ui||U_{i}|, then

−∑iωi|Ui|∑w∑u∈Ui​wlogπθ(ai​u∣xi​u)=−∑iωi|Ui|∑u∈Uilogπθ(ai​u∣xi​u).-\sum_{i}\frac{\omega_{i}}{|U_{i}|}\sum_{w}\sum_{u\in U_{iw}}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{iu}\mid x_{iu})=-\sum_{i}\frac{\omega_{i}}{|U_{i}|}\sum_{u\in U_{i}}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{iu}\mid x_{iu}).

The windowed and original objectives therefore have identical gradients wherever defined.

Proof and implementation scope.

The target sets Ui​wU_{iw} partition UiU_{i}, so each target appears exactly once. With identical conditioning contexts, summing their log-likelihoods over windows gives the full-trajectory sum. Multiplication by the fixed coefficient −ωi/|Ui|-\omega_{i}/|U_{i}| proves equality of the objectives and their gradients. Repeated context has zero loss. A constant positive token credit cancels in the numerator and denominator.

The conditioning assumption is stronger than target conservation. The implemented 256K export retains initial instructions and bounded overlap, so a window can omit earlier context from a longer trajectory. It preserves target counts and fixed normalization but does not generally preserve full-history likelihoods or gradients. The proposition establishes equivalence only when conditioning is unchanged; independently renormalizing each window would also violate its assumptions.

Appendix D DFM-Bench Evaluation Protocol

DFM-Bench evaluates five objects: individual hypotheses, revisions, development paths, research runs, and scientific contributions. This appendix defines their scoring, evidence requirements, and coverage. The version of the rubric and evaluator is retained with each assessment; results from different applicability rules are not pooled without identifying those differences.

D.1 Hypothesis Quality and Automated Review

The hypothesis profile uses eight dimensions: importance, novelty, grounding, falsifiability, data resolvability, feasibility, alternatives, and actionability. Their weights are 20, 20, 15, 10, 10, 10, 10, and 5, respectively, on a 1–10 scale. These are frozen internal protocol conventions, not empirically established optimal weights.

A rubric judge, a domain-scientist role, and a methods-reviewer role assess the same evidence independently of one another’s grades. The current panel uses separate prompts to the same model family. It therefore measures correlated AI perspectives, not three independent expert opinions. Each dimension takes the median when at least two reviewers provide a known score. A complete quality score QQ requires all three reviews, majority eligibility, and all eight dimension medians. The dimension weights sum to 100 and define a weighted mean on the 1–10 scale. Unknown evidence remains unknown rather than becoming zero.

Review packets use source-verbatim cards and traceable supporting material. They distinguish a proposal’s scientific importance from its maturity: an important question need not already have a positive result. Conversely, a completed script does not demonstrate a consequential finding. The packet’s available literature bounds novelty judgments; global novelty is not inferred from limited retrieval.

D.2 Revisions, Development Paths, and Research Runs

Revision evaluation retains the four categorical judgments used by the progress contract. Substantive-progress rates, useful-step rates including repairs, repetition, and insufficient-evidence coverage are reported separately. Numeric Δ​Q=Qchild−Qparent\Delta Q=Q_{\rm child}-Q_{\rm parent} is defined when both automated quality scores are available.

Development-path evaluation assesses explicitly ordered paths. The recorded protocol selects one longest-depth path to each terminal node, breaking ties by identifier, and excludes singleton paths. At crossovers, off-path parents remain context. Coverage therefore counts evaluated paths rather than every possible route through the graph. The seven weights are 5/30/20/20/10/10/5. Research-run evaluation independently inspects the entire graph using weights 25/15/15/20/10/10/5. Both use 0–4 dimension anchors, converted to /100 only under the required completeness and applicability rules.

A legitimately inapplicable dimension differs from an unknown one. Restricted-scope composites are grouped by applicability mask; missing required evidence prevents a full composite. Research-run scores are not averages of development-path scores. Shared ancestors also make path-level measurements correlated, precluding naive independent-sample interpretations.

D.3 Scientific Contribution, Delivery, and Calibration

Scientific-contribution assessment groups related candidates into contribution families and records what was added beyond the starting evidence. Family membership does not imply confirmation; maturity cannot transfer automatically from one member to all others. Negative or inconclusive evidence can matter when it changes an important scientific decision. Human adjudication and independent evidence are needed for stronger claims of novelty and discovery.

Delivery is recorded alongside this scientific profile: proposed, selected, compiled, readiness-passed, executed, and independently reviewed. An unattempted check is distinct from a failure. The protocol does not combine delivery maturity and scientific scores into one overall number.

Calibration concerns the meaning and consistency of judgments. The implemented workflow freezes domain anchors, packets, aggregation, disagreements, and missingness. Same-packet comparisons against fresh-context AI references provide development diagnostics. Human calibration requires independent expert judgments, adjudication, and unseen acceptance cases; it remains pending. Prompt-role agreement alone does not establish validity.

The DFM framework’s distinction between current knowledge progress and future capability growth (Yang et al., 2026b) applies across all five objects. A good final hypothesis does not establish a sound development path, and a disciplined research run does not establish that the trained model improves on future research runs. Frontier plots are useful diagnostics, but a retrospective maximum over final-snapshot scores is monotone by construction and cannot demonstrate learning.

D.4 Development-Path and Research-Run Rubrics

Dimension scores use 0–4 evidence anchors: absent or contradicted, recognized with major gaps, partly substantiated, consistently substantiated, and comprehensive within the declared scope. Domain-specific evidence requirements qualify these anchors. The following labels summarize the clinical rubric; weights are fixed protocol choices rather than calibrated universal utilities.

Dimension Weight Criterion
L1 5% Relevant disciplinary connections
L2 30% Technical and knowledge exploration
L3 20% Cumulative scientific progress
L4 20% Evidential and inferential discipline
L5 10% Scientific continuity and synthesis
L6 10% Adaptive continuation and stopping
L7 5% Efficient use of the path’s budget
Dimension Weight Criterion
T1 25% Disciplinary coverage and integration
T2 15% Technical and knowledge exploration
T3 15% Cumulative scientific progress
T4 20% Evidential and inferential discipline
T5 10% Portfolio synthesis
T6 10% Adaptive scientific decisions
T7 5% Budget-aware exploration

D.5 Assessment Records and Missing Evidence

Each assessment identifies its object, source snapshot, rubric and protocol versions, supporting evidence, scores, rationale, and review status. Hypothesis assessments use a frozen proposal and its evidence. Revisions require actual parent–child pairs; development paths require ordered ancestry; research-run assessment requires the full graph and recorded decisions. Agent trajectories supply evidence about the work behind these objects.

Scores are recorded as known, unknown, or inapplicable under the rubric. Unknown values are not replaced by zero. An incomplete assessment is reported with its coverage and does not receive a complete composite. Resource-allocation judgments require recorded budgets and opportunity information; proposal counts do not reconstruct missing budgets. Contribution records additionally identify the scientific question, the increment beyond starting evidence, and its status as supported, contradicted, inconclusive, or unresolved. Evidence maturity distinguishes proposed, source-grounded, diagnostically examined, study-completed, and independently checked contributions.

D.6 Benchmark Coverage Definitions

Table 1 compares explicit evaluation constructs, not the capabilities of agents that happen to run on a benchmark. Hypothesis merit concerns scientific value and testability; contribution maturity distinguishes proposed, examined, and independently supported contributions. Evidence use concerns grounding analyses or claims in available evidence. Revision assessment compares a change against a predecessor; development-path assessment examines cumulative inquiry; whole-run allocation assesses decisions among research directions. A cross means no explicit assessment under these definitions, not that the benchmark lacks scientific value. Partial coverage identifies a related measure with narrower scope.

AgentIdeaBench scores final ideas with literature-verified critics; its grounding assessment is partial evidence-use coverage. Its generation-time refinement experiments do not constitute an explicit revision or ancestry-path evaluation object (Mo et al., 2026). DiscoveryBench evaluates reference-aligned hypotheses and analytical facets for supplied discovery goals; this provides partial hypothesis-merit and evidence-use coverage, rather than an open-ended merit or contribution-maturity rubric (Majumder et al., 2024). BLADE compares conceptual variables, transformations, and statistical models against expert analyses, providing partial evidence-use coverage through analytical decisions (Gu et al., 2025). ScienceAgentBench assesses generated programs, outputs, and task-stage rubrics; this is partial evidence-use coverage rather than evaluation of evolving scientific claims (Chen et al., 2024).

OEB explicitly assesses evidence, experiments, and responses to contradicted ideas. Its inquiry grouping and search-topology measures supply partial development-path coverage; its budget and concurrency profiles supply partial whole-run allocation coverage because they describe research style without ranking one style above another. It does not supply the proposal-merit or contribution-maturity assessments defined here (Shi et al., 2026). DFM-Bench’s checks indicate implemented rubric coverage conditional on sufficient records, not independent expert validation or empirical superiority over these instruments.

Appendix E Human Assessment Protocol

Human assessment examines the value and design quality of proposed investigations, with automated scores hidden. Overall value, criterion ratings, recommendations, and design-flaw verdicts are separate judgments.

E.1 Review Cohort and Presentation

The review involved 27 medical doctors, medical students, and bioscience PhD students with biomedical or clinical research backgrounds, under three senior supervisors. The fixed hypothesis-atlas cohort contains 292 proposals: HCC (52), MIMIC-IV (60), eICU (60), UK Biobank (55), GEO therapeutic targets (35), and GEO disease mechanisms (30). The groups span the four evaluated life-science domains.

English proposal packets included the scientific question, investigation plan, data requirements, alternative explanations, and citations. Model identity, execution provenance, and automated grades were hidden. Proposals were presented in randomized order, and reviewers assessed each packet without consulting its revision history. Figure 3 illustrates the interface.

E.2 Rating Scales and Recommendations

Reviewers first recorded overall research value on a five-point scale from not worth pursuing to top priority, together with a recommendation to prioritize, revise, defer, or reject. They then rated six criteria on anchored four-point scales: importance, advance over known work, plausible and evidence-bounded claims, data fit, alternative explanations, and informative results. A separate verdict classified consequential design flaws as absent, fixable, or fatal. Reviewers could select “Can’t judge” when evidence or expertise was insufficient; flaw checklists and explanatory comments were optional.

The five-point overall judgment is distinct from the four-point criterion profile. Recommendations to revise or defer do not imply endorsement, and design-flaw verdicts concern the investigation plan.

E.3 Revision Outcomes and Interpretation

The revision analysis compares human-rated quality for a revised hypothesis and its actual predecessor. Positive, zero, and negative score changes define improved, unchanged, and worsened revisions, respectively. The reported mean change and outcome proportions characterize the assessed parent–child pairs. They do not estimate the effect of a model update across independent investigations.

Figure 7 separates criterion profiles and revision outcomes. The MIMIC-IV case (Figure 8) shows six-criterion means along a selected path; it does not imply that all branches improve. Shared ancestry makes revision observations dependent. This assessment is distinct from calibration of the automated evaluator against independently adjudicated, unseen cases.

Appendix F Literature-Inspiration Evaluation

This appendix defines the retrospective literature comparison used in RQ4. “Inspiration” denotes a concrete scientific connection: a reference after the recorded cutoff provides an experimental design, comparator, measurement, or testable evidence gap relevant to developing or testing a generated hypothesis. It does not imply that the publication’s authors encountered the hypothesis or were causally influenced by it.

F.1 Reference Corpus and Temporal Boundaries

One model-blind reference corpus was constructed from deterministic source-only anchors. A completed citation wave followed 420 backward and forward citation traversals, yielding 17,790 citation edges and 16,440 resolved works. The same corpus was available to all model groups within the publication window from 1 April 2025 through 14 October 2026.

References were filtered by each group’s recorded operational cutoff. Exact-day boundaries were retained for GPT serving identifiers. Month-level boundaries were used for Qwen (April 2025, a provisional family proxy), Claude Opus 5 (May 2026), DeepSeek V4.1 (September 2026, a release-month proxy), and GLM-5.3 (August 2026, a release-month proxy). These boundaries make the comparison reproducible; they do not identify internal model knowledge cutoffs.

F.2 Retrieval and Automated Judgment

Candidate retrieval required the best reference card to share at least three non-stopword terms with the hypothesis. This lexical gate determines retrieval eligibility, not semantic relevance. GPT-6 Luna supplied the semantic judgments, with 145 successful judgments from 149 sampled records. Four records lacked successful judgments. Exact duplicate hypothesis–reference inputs shared a judgment, which was propagated to 903 registered hypothesis versions. The resulting labels are correlated automated assessments rather than independent expert reviews.

The inspiration rate uses all generated hypothesis versions as its denominator, as defined in Eq. (7). Only versions receiving a positive judgment contribute to the numerator. Consequently, absence of a positive label may reflect retrieval or audit coverage as well as lack of a qualifying connection. The underlying audit calls this endpoint reference actionability; the report uses the operational term inspiration rate consistently.

F.3 Population Accounting

DiscoveryRSI-27B pools two production runs. The overall numerator and denominator are 74/1,176; domain counts are shown below. The comparison groups are DeepSeek (14/257), GLM (1/36), GPT (59/2,341), and Claude (3/131). Qwen original remains in the underlying audit but is omitted from the main presentation figure.

Group sizes and domain composition differ, and some strata are small. Versions from the same research family and reused judgments are dependent. The report therefore presents descriptive percentages without significance tests.

F.4 Claude Opus 5: Retrieval Sensitivity

The targeted analysis in RQ4 separates retrieval coverage from positive judgments conditional on retrieval. Only 15/131 Claude proposals passed the retrieval gate (11.5%), compared with 355/1,176 DiscoveryRSI proposals (30.2%). Among retrieved proposals, the positive fractions were similar: 20.0% and 20.8%, respectively.

Claude’s median proposal length was 41,134 characters, whereas retrieval used the first 6,000 characters and semantic review used the first 2,500. Provenance and revision notes could therefore displace scientific content. A diagnostic substituted proposal titles as queries while preserving the corpus, scoring method, date rule, and overlap threshold. Claude’s retrieval count increased from 15 to 95. This establishes sensitivity to representation, not additional positive semantic matches. A structured scientific representation and renewed judgments across all groups would be needed to assess the effect on the final comparison.

The audit observes literature correspondence, not researcher exposure, adoption, study initiation, or causal influence. Prospective evaluation would freeze generated hypotheses before researcher review and follow subsequent investigation plans, experiments, and publications.
